concept.name: Record date
concept.definition: The date set by a company's board on which a shareholder must appear on the company's books to receive a declared dividend; shareholders of record are also the ones sent proxy statements, financial reports, and other corporate information.
concept.intuition: It is the company's administrative snapshot: whoever the transfer records show as owner on this date gets the dividend.
concept.mechanics: The board fixes the record date when it declares the dividend. Because trades settle one business day later (T+1), the exchange sets the ex-dividend date on the record date - or the prior business day if the record date falls on a weekend or holiday - making the ex-date, not the record date, the effective trading cutoff.
concept.failure_modes: Confusing the record date with the ex-date causes mistimed trades; with stock dividends and spin-offs the ex-date falls after payment, so selling too early obligates the seller to deliver the extra shares via a due bill.
concept.misconceptions: Buying on the record date does not get you the dividend - settlement timing means you had to buy before the ex-dividend date, which is usually the same day as the record date or earlier.
concept.example: Investor.gov's example: when the record date falls on Sunday March 15, the ex-date moves to Friday March 13, so anyone buying on or after that Friday misses the dividend.
